items.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998
items.q: when Bob did his tributes to Sidney Bechet and he worked with Wynton Marsalis

ctx.x: Well there seems to be some controversy going on in the last few years about the white musicians’ place in jazz today, and whether or not they have usurped the music. And I find it curious that there seems to be very few young black musicians playing what we have come to call classic jazz. At the jazz parties you don’t see many.

That is true. But last year when Bob did his tributes to Sidney Bechet and he worked with Wynton Marsalis, all the musicians with Wynton were totally dedicated to what was going on. I think it’s because they didn’t have an interest in it. It’s not that they couldn’t do it. And I think maybe now they’re becoming more aware of the music. Certainly Michael White loves Johnny Dodds, and would love to play like him. I think that there is also a period of what is young people’s music. It’s not to do with color, it’s to…

Yeah, because we’re getting a couple of generations away from that music now, so it gets harder and harder. If the generation right after the music didn’t get it, what makes you think the next one’s going to? Well you spoke pretty eloquently earlier on about the fact that every generation has its own thing, has to find its own way. I wish we could find a way that the music could be made available, perhaps more available than it is, so that they could make their own choice.
